_comment: COVERAGE INSTRUMENT, NOT A SCORE. The deliverable is the per-module 'uncovered' list -- branches and lines that NEITHER the unit suite NOR the fuzzer reaches -- so a human can decide which are worth aiming a corpus at. A repo-wide percentage is explicitly out of scope; the per-module 'incidental_*_pct' fields exist only to size the uncovered list against its module and are never a target, a threshold, or a gate. The CI job that produces this file MUST NEVER fail on a coverage number -- only on its own infrastructure errors.
_judgements_note: The judgement fields are a CANDIDATE reading produced by the agent that built this instrument. The lead reviews and finalises every one. Until judgements_reviewed is true, treat every judgement as unconfirmed. 'unclassified' means no human judgement is recorded; 'unclassified-stale' means the source at that line changed after a judgement was made and the judgement was refused rather than carried over.

method.tool: gcov (13.3.0) driven directly, parsed with stdlib Python
method.why_not_gcovr_or_lcov: neither is installed; pip refuses gcovr under PEP 668 without --break-system-packages, which would modify the system Python of every machine running this. gcov -j JSON carries per-line and per-branch counts, which is all this instrument needs.
method.merge: the module under test is compiled ONCE into a single coverage-instrumented object linked into BOTH the unit binary and the fuzz binary, so both runs accumulate into the SAME .gcda (gcov counters are additive). This answers 'what does NEITHER reach', not what each reaches separately. Verified: adding the fuzz run moved route.c taken-at-least-once from 92% to 94%.
deviations_from_ci: -O0 instead of CI's -O2/-O1: optimisation merges and elides branches, so an optimised build's gcov mapping does not correspond to source lines a human can judge. -O0 is the standard coverage build.
no ASan/UBSan: sanitizers do not change control flow, only what happens on a bad access, so they cannot change which branches execute.
method.source_lists: copied verbatim from the corresponding .github/workflows/ci.yml steps
method.fuzz_iterations_note: None of the three harnesses accepts an argv or env iteration override (each is main(void) with a compile-time count) and none needs one: the whole suite runs in seconds. No reduced-iteration caveat applies to these numbers.
method.instrumented_scope: ONLY the module under test is compiled with coverage. Harnesses and support modules (shield_action, action_allowlist, shield_learn, control_parser, control_replay, control_ratelimit, hmac_sha256, sha256) are built without it -- this measures the module, not its scaffolding.

uncovered.detail: 1 of 2 branch outcomes on this line never taken (line executed 499773 times)
uncovered.reason: qs_normalize is static with exactly ONE call site (query_shield.c:208), which passes `sizeof norm` where norm is `char norm[QS_NORM_MAX]` -- a compile-time constant 192. norm_size can never be 0.

uncovered.source: for (size_t i = 0; i < len && o + 1 < norm_size; i++) {
uncovered.detail: 1 of 4 branch outcomes on this line never taken (line executed 25621281 times)
uncovered.reason: The never-taken outcome is the WRITE BOUND (`o + 1 < norm_size` false) -- the truncation guard on an untrusted-input buffer. The RAW fuzz mode already feeds 0..256 bytes (fuzz_query_shield.c:145), so it exceeds the 192 buffer and is TRYING to reach this; it fails on statistics, not on structure. MEASURED: a random 256-byte stream normalises to mean 108.5 / max 145 over 2000 samples, against a write bound of 191 -- only ~24% of random byte values are alnum and every non-alnum run collapses to a single space. A 220-byte all-alnum input reaches the bound immediately (verified, no crash). One additional fuzz mode emitting long alphanumeric runs would cover it. Deployed callers cap at CONTROL_QUERY_MAX=172 so this is not a live defect, but it is the write-bound guard and it is currently unexercised.

uncovered.source: for (size_t i = 0; i < nl && nw < QS_MAX_WORDS; ) {
uncovered.detail: 1 of 4 branch outcomes on this line never taken (line executed 56104889 times)
uncovered.reason: The never-taken outcome is the QS_MAX_WORDS=128 cap. norm is at most 191 chars and single-spaced, so the densest possible tokenisation ('a a a ...', 2 chars per word) yields at most 96 words. 96 < 128, so the cap cannot be reached for any input. The header comment states this sizing intent.

uncovered.detail: 1 of 4 branch outcomes on this line never taken (line executed 97176720 times)
uncovered.reason: qs_normalize collapses every run of separators into a SINGLE space and trims leading/trailing spaces, so this skip loop can never iterate twice and can never run off the end of the buffer. The untaken outcome is only reachable against input this function is never handed.

uncovered.detail: 1 of 2 branch outcomes on this line never taken (line executed 51088293 times)
uncovered.reason: The break is dead for the same reason as line 124: trailing spaces are trimmed by qs_normalize, so skipping spaces always lands on a word, never on end-of-string.

uncovered.source: for (int d = c + 1; d <= dhi; d++) {
uncovered.detail: 1 of 2 branch outcomes on this line never taken (line executed 10010 times)
uncovered.reason: The never-taken outcome is loop EXHAUSTION -- the 4th slot never failing to match once slots 1-3 have matched. Only one pattern has a 4th slot ({EMIT, your, system, prompt}). MEASURED: 'print your system prompt' REFUSEs (pattern 10) while 'print your system config' and 'print your system clock' both ALLOW -- so a near-miss that matches EMIT+your+system and then a non-'prompt' word is reachable and simply absent from both corpora. Pairs with line 143.

uncovered.detail: 1 of 2 branch outcomes on this line never taken (line executed 10010 times)
uncovered.reason: The mismatch polarity of the 4th-slot test. In every corpus input that reaches this line the first candidate word matches and returns immediately, so the mismatch-and-continue path never runs. Same one-line fix as 142: a hostile-shaped near-miss ('print your system config') exercises both.

uncovered.detail: 1 of 2 branch outcomes on this line never taken (line executed 453782 times)
uncovered.reason: This UPTIME clause never evaluates true in either corpus. It is live: MEASURED 'since when are you awake' and 'tell me since when' both classify SYSFACTS / SF_UPTIME / rule 3. The corpora simply never use this phrasing. A real deployed classification rule with zero coverage.

uncovered.detail: 1 of 2 branch outcomes on this line never taken (line executed 452254 times)
uncovered.reason: SHADOWED, not dead -- the sharper finding. Every corpus phrasing that would reach this clause also contains 'how long', and rt_seq2("how","long",1) sits EARLIER in the same || chain (line 266) and short-circuits first. MEASURED: 'how long have you been up' matches via the earlier clause, but 'have you been up' (no 'how long') reaches THIS clause and classifies SYSFACTS / SF_UPTIME. Worth a suite case that omits 'how long'.

uncovered.reason: Same short-circuit shadowing as line 268. MEASURED: 'have you been running' reaches this clause and classifies SYSFACTS / SF_UPTIME. Note line 270 ('been','on') IS covered, so the gap is specific to these clauses, not the whole chain.

uncovered.reason: The 'day is' wall-clock DECLINE clause never evaluates true; the 'time is' sibling on the same line is covered. MEASURED: 'what day is it' and 'which day is today' both DECLINE (rule 5), so the clause is live and merely un-exercised.

uncovered.detail: line never executed by either the unit suite or the fuzzer
uncovered.reason: LEAD REVIEW 2026-08-07: reclassified from reachable-worth-fuzzing. UNREACHABLE BY THE FUZZER BY CONSTRUCTION -- route_decline_text() takes NO ARGUMENTS, so no corpus of any shape can reach it; listing it as a fuzz gap would send a future session chasing an impossible case. NOTE THE PRECISE SCOPE, because it is not dead code: it IS genuinely uncovered and it IS live (called at main_x86.c:3713 and :3728, and its exact string is load-bearing in g3_retrieval.h's recall reasoning). The honest disposition is a UNIT-TEST gap in test_route.c, NOT a fuzz gap and NOT dead code. Kept inside the three-value taxonomy deliberately: a fourth category would have to be taught to coverage_report.py's VALID_JUDGEMENTS, and this instrument answers 'can a corpus reach it', for which this judgement is exactly right.

uncovered.reason: LEAD REVIEW 2026-08-07: same as line 367 -- the body of the same zero-argument function. Unreachable by any corpus; a unit-test gap, not a fuzz gap, and not dead code.

uncovered.detail: 4 of 8 branch outcomes on this line never taken (line executed 1514411 times)
uncovered.reason: All four NULL tests never evaluate true across the 22-assert unit suite and 300,020 fuzz iterations. These are caller-contract guards on pointers the single deployed caller (pa_verify_candidate) always supplies non-NULL; a NULL here is a programming error, not attacker-controlled input, so a fuzz corpus is not the right instrument. Cheap to cover with four unit assertions if the lead wants the guard pinned.

uncovered.detail: line never executed by either the unit suite or the fuzzer
uncovered.reason: Body of the NULL guard at line 31 -- unreached for the same reason. Worth noting for the lead that this path dereferences `out` without NULL-checking it, so it would fault if a caller passed out=NULL alongside a NULL frame; that is a latent contract detail the current corpus cannot surface. LEAD VERIFIED 2026-08-07: `out` is dereferenced EIGHT LINES EARLIER (control_verify.c:23-29, the silent-default block) and control_verify.h:82 states `out` MUST be non-NULL. So this is a documented precondition consistently applied, NOT an inconsistency -- the guard checks the four pointers whose NULLness is a caller error it can still report through `out`. No defect.
